description: Mistakes made, and what changed so they cannot recur. Every entry must name a concrete safeguard — a rule, a test, a check — not merely an intention to be careful.
why: A mistake that produces only an apology will happen again. A mistake that produces a test will not. This file is the audit trail of that conversion, and reading it is part of onboarding.
rules_for_this_file: Add an entry the moment an error is found, not later.
'safeguard' must be something executable or checkable. 'Be more careful' is not a safeguard.
Never delete an entry. A corrected mistake is still evidence of a weak spot.
If the same root cause appears twice, the safeguard was inadequate — say so and strengthen it.

lessons.title: Rent TDS deducted when none was due
lessons.what_happened: ₹3,000 was deducted under s.194I on rent of ₹30,000/month. The annual total (₹3,60,000) was compared against the ₹50,000 threshold, but that threshold is PER MONTH. ₹30,000/month is below it, so no TDS was ever due.
lessons.root_cause: Threshold basis was carried in prose, where per-month and per-year read alike.
lessons.cost: ₹3,000 wrongly withheld from the landlord, a challan filed under the wrong year, and a Q1 return that had to include a deduction that should not have existed.
lessons.safeguard: vm/rules/tds-in.json encodes threshold_basis explicitly ('per_month'). vm/rules/tds_engine.py refuses to compare a monthly-basis threshold against an annual total, and states in its explanation that 'annualised X is NOT the test'. Covered by a self-test case that fails if the behaviour regresses.

lessons.title: A vendor paid gross for four consecutive years
lessons.what_happened: Professional fees to the auditor were paid without TDS across FY2022-23 to FY2025-26 — roughly ₹4,71,000 of payments and ₹47,000 of undeducted TDS. Nobody was tracking the cumulative total per vendor.
lessons.root_cause: No monitoring. The rule was never in doubt; the running total was simply never computed.
lessons.cost: ~₹47,000 of TDS plus interest, spread across years now largely beyond correction.
lessons.safeguard: vm/rules/monitor.py computes year-to-date totals per vendor per section and flags 'breached-undeducted' and 'approaching' before the next payment. --check-payment answers 'what happens if I pay this?' BEFORE the money moves.
lessons.verified: monitor.py --check-payment on the live register returns the correct net-payable

lessons.title: Professional advice conflicted with the statute and was followed
lessons.what_happened: The firm's own tax team computed TDS of ₹12,500 plus ₹750 interest, then 73 minutes later withdrew it: 'tax is not deducted since the company already has significant accumulated losses'. Losses do not remove a deductor's liability under s.201 — they affect only the s.40(a)(ia) disallowance.
lessons.root_cause: Two distinct consequences of non-deduction were conflated, and the advice came from the party being paid.
lessons.cost: ₹12,500 plus accruing interest, and a fourth year added to the pattern in L002.
lessons.safeguard: tds-in.json records under 'penalty-non-deduction' that the 30% disallowance is a CONSEQUENCE of not deducting, never an alternative to it, and that the deductor remains liable under s.201 regardless of either party's losses. Roadmap phase 6 makes conflicts between advice and encoded rules visible rather than silently resolved.

lessons.title: The assistant asserted a fact it had not checked
lessons.what_happened: Asked which section a ₹980 default related to, the assistant answered 'rent TDS' by reasoning from a pattern seen in a different financial year. The bank statement showed no rent TDS in FY2024-25 at all. The operator asked 'are you sure? how did you find out?' and the claim collapsed.
lessons.root_cause: Pattern-matching substituted for retrieval, and the answer was stated with the same confidence as verified findings.
lessons.cost: None — caught immediately. Had it not been challenged, it would have driven a payment under the wrong section code.
lessons.safeguard: Two things. (1) Every answer about a fact must cite the document, bank line or voucher it came from; an uncited claim is a defect. (2) The coverage table (kb migration 003) makes 'I hold no evidence for that' an available and expected answer. Recorded in docs/compliance-safety-net.md as an explicit limit of the assistant, with the operator's challenge named as a control that works.
lessons.verified: docs/compliance-safety-net.md, section 'Four limits worth stating plainly', item 3

lessons.title: A migration recorded itself as applied when it had failed
lessons.what_happened: Migration 002 added a pgvector column. On a server without the extension it failed — but psql continued past the error and still inserted the schema_version row, so the schema history claimed a migration that had not run.
lessons.root_cause: psql continues after errors unless ON_ERROR_STOP is set, and the migration was not wrapped in a transaction.
lessons.cost: None in production; found during testing. Would have caused silent divergence between recorded and actual schema.
lessons.safeguard: Migrations run with -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1, migration 002 is wrapped in BEGIN/COMMIT so a failure rolls back its own version row, and kb-setup.ps1 re-queries schema_version after running rather than trusting the exit code.
lessons.verified: kb-setup.ps1 reports 'migration 002 skipped (needs pgvector)' and schema_version correctly omits version 2

lessons.title: Document classification silently ignored the project's own filenames
lessons.what_happened: Regex word boundaries (\b) treat _ and - as word characters, so '\bchallan\b' did not match '2026-05-07_challan.pdf' — exactly the naming convention ADR-0012 prescribes. Scanned documents with no extractable text were left unclassified and invisible to type filters.
lessons.root_cause: A regex assumption never tested against a real filename.
lessons.cost: 34 documents unfindable by type in a 291-document corpus. No external consequence, but the search would have quietly under-reported for months.
lessons.safeguard: Separators are normalised to spaces before matching, the filename is searched before the body, and vm/kb/test_ingest.py has a case asserting a scanned challan classifies from its filename alone.

lessons.title: Statement parser invented transactions from page furniture
lessons.what_happened: Loading a real FD statement produced 6 'transactions', two of which were not transactions at all: a printed timestamp ('Date And Time : 09/03/2026 12.44 PM') became a ₹12.44 line, and a 'Lien Balance: 0.00' footer became a zero-value line. Both contained a date and a decimal number, which was the only test applied.
lessons.root_cause: The parser accepted any line containing a date and a number. Statement footers and headers satisfy that trivially.
lessons.cost: None — caught on the first real run. But an invented transaction is the one parsing error that cannot be recovered by re-reading, because nothing downstream can tell it apart from a genuine one.
lessons.safeguard: vm/rules/reconcile.py adds NOISE_RE rejecting timestamps, balance/lien footers, page furniture and totals, plus a rule that at least one amount must be greater than zero. Every pattern in NOISE_RE comes from an observed false positive, and vm/rules/test_reconcile.py asserts both that the noise lines are rejected and that the real transactions on the same page still parse.

lessons.title: Statement loader reported 'no transactions' for a statement full of them
lessons.what_happened: A full-year statement containing hundreds of transactions parsed to zero. The PDF extracts as fragmented text with dates and amounts on separate lines ('TAX:0.8,080.00 5,31,763.'), which the line-based parser cannot match. It reported '0 transactions' and moved on.
lessons.root_cause: The parser had no way to distinguish 'this period had no activity' from 'I cannot read this layout', and reported both identically.
lessons.cost: None yet — caught in testing. In use it would have been worse than a crash: coverage would show the year as loaded, the evidence report would show 100% completeness, and a year of transactions would be invisible while every indicator said fine.
lessons.safeguard: vm/rules/reconcile.py adds diagnose_text(), which counts lines carrying dates versus amounts and names the actual cause — fragmented layout needing a table-aware extractor, a scan needing OCR, or an unsupported date format. The loader refuses to mark coverage 'held' when nothing parsed, so the year stays visibly 'missing'. Covered by test_reconcile.py::TestDiagnostics.
lessons.verified: test_reconcile.py::TestDiagnostics, and run against the real FY2025-26 statement: reports '306 lines have a date, 281 have an amount, but none have both'

lessons.title: Hand-rolled coordinate extraction looked successful while missing a third of the statement
lessons.what_happened: A coordinate-aware extractor pulled 240 transactions from a statement that line parsing could not read at all — every row dated, every row with an amount, descriptions correct, balances plausible. Cross-checking against three transactions known to be in that period found only one: the ₹1,47,500 ARTH audit fee and the ₹5,50,000 salary-arrears TDS were both absent, and only 9 of 12 monthly rent challans appeared.
lessons.root_cause: Two causes. The statement interleaves two accounts (current and FD) so a single running-balance chain does not apply; and the anchor heuristic requires a date and an amount in the movement column on the SAME visual row, which some layouts split differently. Neither was visible from internal consistency alone.
lessons.cost: None — caught before use. Had it been trusted, reconciliation would have reported clean exceptions while a third of the year's transactions were simply absent, and evidence completeness would have shown a high percentage against an incomplete population.
lessons.safeguard: vm/rules/pdf_table.py adds cross_check(), which verifies that transactions known to exist in a period were actually extracted, and the module docstring states plainly that balance continuity proves internal consistency but NOT completeness. The extractor is documented as ASSISTIVE — its output must be cross-checked against known transactions before any period is marked verified, and it does not mark coverage 'held' by itself. Superseded in practice: vm/rules/pdf_table.py now tries pdfplumber FIRST and falls back to coordinates only when no table is recoverable. The wider lesson stands and is why the regression was caught at all.
lessons.verified: cross_check() against the FY2025-26 statement reports the two missing payments by name
lessons.outcome_2026_07_29: RESOLVED by using a real table extractor. pdfplumber recovers the statement's actual ruled table with clean columns, giving 299 transactions (matching the count the existing reconciliation engine independently handled for this year), all with balances, and cross_check() reporting ALL FOUND. The coordinate approach is retained only as a fallback for PDFs with no recoverable table, and is documented as assistive.
lessons.general_lesson: Balance continuity proves internal consistency, not completeness. Only checking for transactions you already know exist catches a silently incomplete extraction. Equally: reach for the right library before hand-rolling geometry — four rounds of heuristic tuning were spent on a problem pdfplumber solves outright.

lessons.title: Tally report IDs silently ignore the requested date range
lessons.what_happened: A 'Day Book' export returned byte-identical output (850,261 chars) for all eleven financial years. Querying one bank ledger this way suggested ~96 vouchers existed across a decade, and a written finding claimed '97% of bank transactions are unrecorded'.
lessons.root_cause: Tally answers from its CURRENT PERIOD. SVFROMDATE/SVTODATE on a report ID are advisory; the loaded period wins.
lessons.fix: Use a Collection with SVCURRENTCOMPANY + SVCURRENTDATE alongside SVFROMDATE/SVTODATE. FY2019-20 then returned 3,106 vouchers instead of 0. Full extract: 10,135 vouchers.
lessons.generalisation: Identical output sizes across different query parameters means the parameter is being ignored. Always vary an input and confirm the output varies before trusting a negative result.

lessons.title: An absent finding was published as a finding
lessons.what_happened: '~3% of bank transactions are recorded in Tally' was written into a verification document and framed as confirming a pattern of poor bookkeeping. It was a query artefact; the books hold 10,135 balanced vouchers.
lessons.root_cause: An empty/small result was interpreted as evidence of absence in the world, rather than as possible evidence of a broken query. Three caveats were listed but the headline number was still asserted.
lessons.fix: Retracted in TALLY-VS-BANK-FIRST-PASS.md. Before reporting that something is MISSING, positively verify the retrieval path works by finding something known to exist.
lessons.generalisation: Absence of evidence from a tool is first a claim about the tool. Accusations about records demand a working reader before they are made.

lessons.title: abs() on amounts broke 22 genuine vouchers
lessons.what_happened: 22 vouchers failed the double-entry check. They looked like data-quality problems in the books.
lessons.root_cause: Tally records contra lines as a NEGATIVE amount on a side (e.g. forex revaluation: a -11,204.00 credit). Taking abs() turned a subtraction into an addition.
lessons.fix: Preserve sign when the AMOUNT sign disagrees with ISDEEMEDPOSITIVE. All 10,135 vouchers then balanced.
lessons.generalisation: A validation failure is a bug in the validator until proven otherwise. Do not report the source data as faulty until the reader is proven correct.

lessons.title: Substring vendor search merged four unrelated vendors
lessons.what_happened: Searching 'ARTH' returned Kritarth Consulting, Parth Cooling Solutions and Siddharth Enterprises alongside ARTH & Associates, inflating that vendor's totals.
lessons.root_cause: ILIKE '%term%' has no word boundary.
lessons.fix: Word-boundary regex (\m...\M), with substring hits offered only as 'did you mean'.
lessons.generalisation: For money totals attributed to a named party, a loose match is worse than no match: it produces a confident wrong number.

lessons.title: A literal % in SQL was eaten as a psycopg placeholder
lessons.what_happened: The 'tds' command reported no TDS ledgers at all, while TDS - PROFESSIONAL FEES plainly existed with hundreds of entries.
lessons.root_cause: ILIKE '%TDS%' written inline; psycopg treats % as parameter interpolation.
lessons.fix: Pass LIKE patterns as bound parameters.
lessons.generalisation: Same family as L010/L011 — an empty result that felt like an answer. Any zero-row result on a question expected to have rows must be challenged before it is reported.

lessons.title: Non-accounting voucher types were loaded into financial totals
lessons.what_happened: 33 Memorandum vouchers carrying Rs 5.9 crore were extracted and counted alongside real vouchers, inflating FY2016-17 to FY2018-19. They all passed the double-entry balance check, so no existing validation caught them.
lessons.root_cause: The extractor took every voucher the gateway returned. Tally's Memorandum type is deliberately NON-ACCOUNTING - it never enters the books - and ISCANCELLED/ISOPTIONAL were likewise never checked.
lessons.fix: Exclude Memorandum/memo types and any voucher flagged ISDELETED, ISCANCELLED or ISOPTIONAL. Count went 10,135 -> 10,102.
lessons.generalisation: Passing an internal consistency check does not mean a record BELONGS in the dataset. Validity and relevance are different tests; ask 'should this be here at all' separately from 'is this well-formed'. Found only because the user asked what was missing rather than accepting a completeness claim.

lessons.title: XML numeric entity mistaken for a control character
lessons.what_happened: Tally's synthetic root group arrives as the literal text ' Primary'. Code stripped \x00-\x1f expecting a real control byte, which matched nothing, so every ledger walked up to the root: 61 of 66 unmapped and the whole balance sheet collapsed into one bucket.
lessons.root_cause: Assumed the escape had been resolved into a byte. It had not - it was still five characters of text.
lessons.fix: Strip numeric character references as text (&#\d+;) before stripping control bytes; stop the group walk one level below the root.
lessons.generalisation: When a name looks like it contains an escape, print its repr() before writing code against it. Assuming a decode step happened is how a parser silently matches nothing.

lessons.title: Double-counted profit in the balance sheet
lessons.what_happened: The generated balance sheet was out by exactly the profit figure. The profit was added to Equity even though Tally's Reserve & Surplus closing balance already contains it.
lessons.root_cause: Applied a textbook rule (carry profit to reserves) without checking whether the source had already applied it. The trial balance summing to zero on balance-sheet ledgers alone was the available evidence and it was overlooked.
lessons.fix: Use Tally's Reserve & Surplus balance as-is; report profit only in the P&L.
lessons.generalisation: A discrepancy EXACTLY equal to a figure already in play is almost always double-counting, not a missing entry. Check whether the source already did the step before doing it again.

lessons.title: 'Needs a CA' used to excuse work that was merely hard
lessons.what_happened: Depreciation, provisions, tax, notes and the audit opinion were excluded from the generated financials as a single group 'those need the CA'. The user challenged it. On examination, depreciation (Schedule II lives are published law), most notes (prescribed disaggregation tables), and current tax (law plus ledger data) were all computable. Only deferred tax, contingent liabilities, actuarial valuations, going concern and the audit opinion genuinely need judgement.
lessons.root_cause: Collapsed five different things into one exclusion and presented a capability gap as a professional boundary. The real reason was that they are harder to build.
lessons.fix: Built fixed_assets.py (Schedule II depreciation with per-asset workings), notes.py (Schedule III notes), tax_computation.py (disallowances + regime comparison). Each states exactly which inputs it cannot derive and leaves those blank.
lessons.generalisation: When declining scope, name the specific blocker for each item. 'Needs an expert' covering several things at once is usually hiding at least one item that is merely difficult. The honest test: is the missing input a LAW, a LEDGER, or a BELIEF? Only beliefs need the human.

lessons.title: Assumed WDV depreciation and nearly reported a 6-lakh error that did not exist
lessons.what_happened: The Fixed Asset Register computed 13,11,896 of depreciation against 7,03,508 booked - an apparent 6.08 lakh under-provision, which would have gone to the CA as a serious finding. The company uses the STRAIGHT LINE method. Under SLM the computation matched to 137 rupees on 7.03 lakh (0.02%), and to 23 rupees in FY2024-25. There was no error at all.
lessons.root_cause: WDV was hard-coded as the default. Schedule II permits either method and does not prescribe one. WDV vs SLM differs by roughly 2x in early years - exactly the magnitude that looks like a serious under-provision.
lessons.fix: detect_method() computes both and keeps whichever matches what was booked; --method defaults to 'auto'. The report shows both candidates and states which matched, so the basis is visible rather than assumed.
lessons.generalisation: Before reporting that someone's figure is wrong, check whether a DIFFERENT PERMITTED ASSUMPTION reproduces it. Where a standard allows several treatments, infer which one is in use from the data instead of defaulting. A ~2x discrepancy is a strong hint of a method mismatch, not an error.

lessons.title: Charged depreciation on gross cost where accumulated depreciation sat in separate ledgers
lessons.what_happened: Asset ledgers hold ORIGINAL COST permanently (3D Printer stays at 13,35,000 every year) because the company keeps accumulated depreciation in separate 'Accumulated Depn : ...' ledgers. Applying a WDV rate to that gross figure over-charges every year after the first.
lessons.root_cause: Assumed the asset ledger balance was the written-down value. Gross-block accounting is at least as common.
lessons.fix: Net the block's accumulated depreciation off, apportioned across assets by cost, before applying a WDV rate. SLM correctly continues to charge on original cost.
lessons.generalisation: Check whether a balance is gross or net before computing on it. Two ledgers that must be read together are easy to read singly.
